label: Unit 1
themeSub: What's inside, and what it does
intro: Kids get taught tummy and boo-boo and then spend a year unlearning both. This unit gives him the real word the first time — stomach, lungs, heart, bones — and one true sentence about what each one does, because a name with no job attached is just a longer word. It also gives him the two things a doctor's visit actually asks of him: point at where it hurts, and say what happened.

gelds.text: Names the part instead of pointing at it
Says what a part DOES, not only what it's called
Knows inside from outside, and that inside still belongs to him
Can say where it hurts and what happened, to somebody who isn't us
Sequences a hygiene routine without being walked through it

tryNote: Three or four minutes each. The bath and the bandage are the two best moments for this — he's already looking at the part in question.

daily.title: Name it, don't point at it
daily.do: Wash an arm and name it. Wash the knee, the elbow, the shoulder. He says the word back before you move on — pointing doesn't count.
daily.stretch: Ask what's UNDER what you're washing. Under the knee is a bone. Under the arm is muscle. Inside the chest is the heart, and it's going right now.

daily.title: Find your own heartbeat
daily.do: Hand on his chest, sitting still. Then twenty jumping jacks and hand on the chest again. "What's different?" Let him say fast — don't say it for him.
daily.stretch: Ask WHY it went fast. He doesn't need the right answer; he needs to guess out loud that his body needed something. Then tell him: the heart pushes blood, and running needs more of it.
daily.skill: Cause and effect inside his own body

daily.title: Where and what happened
daily.do: Any bump from the day, ask two questions in this order: where does it hurt, and what happened. Both answers out loud, in words.
daily.stretch: Make him tell it to somebody else at the table, start to finish, without you filling in the middle. That's the version a doctor gets.
daily.skill: Reporting his own body to a stranger

goalsTitle: What he should have by the end of this unit

his: Says stomach, lungs, heart, bones, muscles — and one thing each of them does
Points to where his heart is without checking your face first
Knows which parts are inside him and that he can't see them
Tells somebody else where it hurts and what happened, unprompted
Washes his hands in the right order, all five steps, on his own

weekend: Next time anybody in the house takes medicine or puts on a bandage, narrate it: what it's for, what it does, why we're doing it now. He's watching that anyway — he might as well get the words.

songs.title: My Body Works
songs.style: A bouncy, happy preschool sing-along with marimba, ukulele and hand claps. Slow, steady tempo a four-year-old can sing with, one warm friendly voice, a simple repeated melody, every word clear. Singing starts within the first two seconds, and it ends cleanly with no long outro.
lyrics: My heart goes pump, pump, pump,
My lungs fill up with air —
breathe in and let it out.
My bones hold me up tall,
and works on it all day.
and they work all day for me!

advanced.label: Heart
advanced.note: Your heart pushes blood all the way around you, even while you sleep.

advanced.label: Lungs
advanced.note: You have two lungs, and they fill up with air every time you breathe in.

advanced.label: Brain
advanced.note: Your brain tells the rest of you what to do.

advanced.label: Stomach
advanced.note: Your tummy's real name is your stomach. Your food goes there first.

advanced.label: Bones
advanced.note: Your bones hold you up. You have more than two hundred of them.

advanced.label: Muscles
advanced.note: Muscles pull on your bones. That is how you move.

advanced.label: Blood
advanced.note: Blood carries food and air to every part of you.

advanced.label: Tongue
advanced.note: Your tongue tastes your food and helps you make words.

sort.title: Inside or Outside?
sort.yesSay: Yes. That one is inside you.
sort.noSay: Right. That one is on the outside.
sort.retry: Have another think. Could you see it in the mirror?

items.note: You can't see it, but you can feel it going.
Outside, which is why it's the one that gets scraped.
Two of them, right behind your ribs.
Outside. It's the only part you can cut without it hurting.
Inside, holding you up the whole time.
Outside, and they keep dust out of your eye.
Inside your head, behind the hardest bone you have.
Outside. They grow the whole time and you never feel it.
Inside — and when you see it, that means something opened up.
Outside, but it's the mark of a tube that fed you from the inside.
Outside. Smile in the mirror and there they are.
Inside, and it's a bag, not the front of you.
Outside. Stick it out and you can see it in the mirror.
Inside, under your skin — but you can watch them move from outside.
Outside. It's the wrapper that keeps everything else in.
Inside. Press on your chest and you can feel them under there.
Outside. Bend your arm and there it is.
Inside. You feel your food go down it, but you never see it.

sort.title: Good for My Body?
sort.yesSay: Yes. That is good for your body.
sort.noSay: Right. That one is not good for your body.
sort.retry: Think about how your body would feel after.

items.text: You drank water when you were thirsty.
items.note: Thirsty is your body asking. Water is the answer.

items.text: You washed your hands before dinner.
items.note: Germs are too small to see. That's the whole reason we wash.

items.text: You stayed up so late you were tired all day.
items.note: Sleep is when your body does the fixing.

items.text: You ate something green at dinner.
items.note: You don't have to love it. Your body still uses it.

items.text: You ran around outside for a long time.
items.note: Your heart gets stronger every time you make it work.

items.text: You rubbed your eyes with dirty hands.
items.note: That's the shortest trip germs can take to get inside you.

items.text: You brushed your teeth before bed.
items.note: The sugar that stays on all night is what makes holes.

items.text: You had candy instead of dinner.
items.note: Candy has no job to do. Dinner does.

items.text: You told a grown-up your tummy hurt.
items.note: Nobody can help with something they don't know about.

items.text: You kept playing on a hurt foot and didn't tell anybody.
items.note: Being tough about it makes it take longer to get better.

items.text: You wore your helmet on your bike.
items.note: Your skull is hard. The helmet is for the day that isn't enough.

items.text: You shared a drink with a kid who was coughing.
items.note: Sharing is kind. Sharing germs is the one exception.

items.text: You sat still for the doctor even though you didn't want to.
items.note: Hard, and still the right call. Being still is how they find things out.

items.text: You took medicine somebody handed you at school.
items.note: Only a grown-up in our family gives you medicine. Nobody else, ever.
Your body runs on food. Breakfast is the first fill-up of the day.
Your elbow catches the germs so nobody else has to.

items.text: You picked at a scab until it bled.
items.note: Under a scab, your skin is busy fixing. Picking makes it start over.

items.text: You said no to dessert because your tummy was already full.
items.note: Full is your body saying stop. Listening to it is the hard part.

steps.text: Scrub while you sing the song
Brush the top and the bottom
Rinse the brush and stand it up
Take the vitamin a grown-up gave you
The doctor listens to your heart
